opp_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the email alias list for setting up email routing on my company domain. This is the planning step before configuring forwarding rules in a service like Cloudflare Email Routing, Google Workspace, ImprovMX, or my domain registrar's email forwarding feature.

First, ask me for: (1) my domain name, (2) the departments/functions in my company that need a dedicated alias (e.g., support, billing, sales, hello, info, legal, security, hr, careers, press), and (3) the real inbox(es) each alias should forward to (e.g., a personal Gmail, a shared Google Workspace inbox, a helpdesk tool address).

Using my answers, produce a clear, organized alias-routing plan as a table or list with three columns: Alias (e.g., support@mydomain.com), Destination inbox (the real email address it forwards to), and Purpose/notes (why this alias exists, who monitors it, or any special handling like auto-forward vs. catch-all).

Include common, generally-recommended aliases even if I didn't mention them (support, billing, admin, security, abuse) and flag any that are missing but typically expected for a company domain, so I can decide whether to add them.

Do not attempt to configure DNS records, MX records, or actually set up forwarding — this step is only about producing the definitive alias list and destination mapping that will be used in the next configuration step.

When done, report back the finalized alias table, note any aliases I explicitly declined to include, and list any open questions (e.g., destinations I haven't decided on yet) that need my input before routing can be configured.

opp_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me configure email routing rules at {{vendor}}, the email provider for our company domain, so that role-based aliases (e.g. hello@, support@, founders@) forward to the correct real inboxes or teammates.

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: our domain name, the list of aliases we want to create and which real inbox or teammate each should route to, and confirmation that {{vendor}} is our configured provider with access already set up under my configured credentials.

Once you have this, use {{vendor}}'s dashboard or API to:
1. Create each alias/masked address on our domain.
2. Set up routing rules so each alias forwards mail to the correct real inbox(es) or is assigned to the right teammate, making ownership explicit.
3. Where {{vendor}} supports it, configure automation so rules trigger actions on events (e.g. auto-assign, auto-forward, auto-tag) rather than requiring manual sorting.
4. Verify that any existing catch-all or default routing won't conflict with the new rules.

Test the setup by checking {{vendor}}'s rule list/preview (or sending a test message if that's low-risk) to confirm each alias routes to the intended destination.

Done looks like: every requested alias exists, each has an explicit routing rule pointing to the correct inbox or teammate, any automation rules are active, and there are no conflicting or orphaned rules.

Report back with: the list of aliases created, their routing destinations, any automation rules configured, and any aliases you could not fully set up (with the reason, e.g. missing inbox target or permission issue). If any DNS-level change (like adding an MX or forwarding record) is required and hasn't already been done, flag it clearly since that remains a human step if it involves changes outside {{vendor}}'s dashboard scope.

opp_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me configure DNS records to enable email routing on our company domain via {{vendor}}, our edge-platform DNS provider. Please do the following:

1. If you don't already have it, ask me for: (a) the company domain name, (b) confirmation that {{vendor}} is the DNS provider managing this domain's zone, and (c) the specific MX record values (mail server hostnames and priority numbers) and the SPF record text value that should be applied — these typically come from the email routing feature's setup instructions in the {{vendor}} dashboard, so check there first if I haven't supplied them.

2. Using my configured credentials, access the {{vendor}} dashboard or API for the domain's DNS zone.

3. Add the required MX records (with correct priority/hostname values) so mail for the domain routes correctly.

4. Add or update the SPF TXT record with the correct value to authorize the mail routing service, being careful not to create a duplicate SPF record if one already exists — merge values into a single SPF TXT record if needed.

5. Save the changes and verify the records appear correctly in the zone (query the DNS via the dashboard's record viewer or a DNS lookup tool to confirm the MX and SPF/TXT records are present and correctly formatted).

6. Note that DNS propagation is a third-party process outside your control — full propagation and activation across the internet remains a human step (i.e., a waiting/monitoring step, not something you can force to completion). You may check back and report visible propagation status if asked.

When done, report back: the exact MX and SPF record values you added, confirmation that they saved successfully in {{vendor}}'s DNS zone, and the current propagation/verification status you observed. Flag any conflicts (e.g., existing MX or SPF records) you encountered and how you resolved them.

opp_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me verify email routing on our company domain. Email aliases (e.g., info@, hello@, support@, sales@ — ask me for the exact list of aliases and the real destination inboxes they should forward to if I haven't provided them yet) have already been configured to forward to real inboxes. Your job now is to test and confirm that forwarding actually works.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for: the domain name, the full list of aliases to test, and the destination inbox(es) where forwarded mail should land, plus confirmation you have access to send/check mail using my configured credentials (e.g., via an email client or webmail already connected).
2. For each alias, send a distinct, clearly labeled test email (include the alias name and a timestamp in the subject line so results aren't confused) to that alias address.
3. Check the corresponding destination inbox(es) for arrival of each test message. Allow a few minutes and recheck if a message hasn't arrived immediately, including checking spam/junk folders.
4. Record results in a simple table: alias tested, destination inbox, delivered (yes/no), time to delivery, and any bounce or error message received.
5. If any alias fails to deliver, note the exact bounce/error text and flag it — do not attempt to change DNS or routing configuration yourself; just report the failure clearly.

Done looks like: every alias on the list has been tested with a unique message, and you have a complete results table showing delivery status for each one, with failures clearly flagged and their error details captured.

Report back with: the results table, a summary count of successes vs. failures, and the raw bounce/error text for any failed alias so I can address the underlying configuration.
